Question: How does a book editor edit digital manuscripts (is that a dichotomy)? How are words crossed out, notes/comments added, and all the traditional marks and symbols used, which used to be done in red pencil on paper, now done on digital submissions?
Answer: As to your main question, most book editors do so electronically these days. For a long time, I did it in two stages, first on my kindle using highlights and codes, and then transferring that to my PC and converting the codes into headings, before writing up comments individually where necessary. But there are a number of platforms on which you can add a full range of annotations that we would, in previous days, have done in blue pencil - because that was what the final decisionmaker in an editorial team would use. I used to use green ink if I was passing on my corrections to another editor, so that the other editor could use blue. Today, you can still do this. I’m aware of editorial teams that do so using software, using, as you put it, all the traditional marks and symbols (I don’t know what the software is called) but it makes it very easy to see who has corrected what, and different colours ensure that, for example, a proofreader who is checking only for typesetting errors (errors introduced during the process of preparation for print) is not also marking up typographical or punctuation errors which are the preserve of a different editor. Authors still write “stet” next to editor’s corrections when they mean to insist that what they originally wrote should be kept. As to your parenthesis: Speaking as a book editor… no it’s not a dichotomy. I wonder if you meant a “contradiction in terms” and no, it’s not that either; a manuscript is a draft that the author considers good enough to share with someone else. Its etymology is “handwritten” but etymology isn’t meaning. That’s not what it means now. (A dichotomy is a thing, usually abstract, that is divided, or divides or is split, into two._

Question: I was asked this question at a job interview: “Suppose we hire you and your first job is to fire 20% of people in your department. How do you find out who's doing nothing?” How would you decide who to fire?
Answer: It’s not done by finding out who is doing nothing. First, you clarify; are they looking for a 20% reduction in payroll, or do they want a 20% reduction in actual staff, and if the latter, what saving are they hoping to make in payroll. It depends a lot on the type of employee and the business you’re in but the difference can be pretty major. Second, your goal has to be that your team/department/service/line or whatever has to be functional after the downsizing. Being functional means it still contains all the necessary skills, AND it’s a group of people capable of working together. Sometimes, this also means the most productive people. But often it doesn’t. You might well find you need to keep someone less productive because they have a skill no one else has, or they have a great rapport with a client or vendor, or they have long experience that’s occasionally very valuable but most of the time they’re kinda slow. Or it’s just that everyone else really likes them, so keeping them means keeping the team together. Seriously, the managers that fail at this task are the ones who consider their employees individually. The ones who assess the whole group, and seek the aid of the group in making the tough decisions, are the ones who succeed. Of course, you might do everything right and still fail. Sometimes a 20% cut is just too much, and it kills the department. It’s not always going to be possible to tell beforehand. So step #1 in the process is to polish up your CV/resume, and start sending it out. You might make a success of this massive cut. But if the company is telling you to cut a 5th of your workforce/payroll, the company is probably not in great health. Maybe this cut is exactly what it will need, and you’ll be a hero. But probably not. IF asked this in an interview, I would tell them ALL of the above. And I would expect their job offer to come with some really, really attractive terms.

Question: Why can't future continuous and perfect continuous be changed into passive voice?
Answer: The issue here is not of the relationship between active and passive versions of tenses. “Changing” from active to passive is only useful to lazy teachers who need an exercise to give to their students to make both feel like they are working. That just isn't how voice works in English Voice is sometimes a choice: choosing active or passive enables you to redirect attention to a different object, for whatever reason: She didn't jump in front of that train; the train jumped its rails and [it] hit her. She testified to how she had been abused by the defendant. In both these examples, active and passive have been chosen to align with a structured thought. There are also cases where only active or passive is possible: The sun shone. My house was built in 1900. “Shine” when it means “produce light” cannot have an object, so must be active. In the second example, the agent of the verb is unknown, so the patient has to become the “subject” of the sentence. So thought experiment: take that obligate passive and make it imperfective (“continuous”). From 1897 to 1900 my house was being built. Same, in the present: At the moment , my house is being built What do you notice about these two passives? The auxiliary “is” serves to indicate the time of the verb. Some argue that this isn't passive at all, because we are describing the state of the house as “being built” but that isn't what “passive” means. Passive is when the agent is not the subject. In both sentences, we still don't know the agent. English is confusing because tense is not tightly bound to the construction of the verb. This time next year, my house will be being built. If I add an agent, this can be expressed in the active voice: This time next year, I will be building my house. But to do this I have added information that wasn't there before. I won't attempt to address whatever you might mean by “future continuous.” Depending on where you study English, there are different ways of describing different tenses (many of which, native speakers do not bother to name) and some of the names given are, as in this case seeming to attempt to describe both the construction (what particles are used to create the tense) and the usage at the same time, and result in self contradictions like “perfect continuous” and pleonasms like “past perfect.”

Question: How come people get self-conscious about their accent when they are speaking a language that is foreign to them?
Answer: This is for me. My most regular class is teaching English to French adults who have been failed by the French education system. That is to say, most of them had a total of 9 years of English at school and they are barely better than beginners. Among the difficulties they face is a whole host of lies they were told by teachers. Probably the worst one is “English is easy.” This lie is backed up by all sorts of spurious arguments, and children are easily convinced of it. So when they fail, over and over again, at their English tests, they come to the perfectly reasonable conclusion that they must be stupid or “have no gift for languages.” Sadly, many of their parents come to the same conclusion. When I tell my adult students that no, English is a) objectively difficult and b) for a variety of reasons, especially challenging for monolingual French speakers, they are both reassured and encouraged. They recognize this will take effort, rather than some knack or gift for languages that they, magically and arbitrarily lack. Haven’t finished ranting. Because another lie they are told is that in order to make themselves understood (and be respected), they must learn to speak with a “good accent.” Sometimes (worse still) they are told they have to speak English with an “authentic” accent. Now, given that human’s main fear in communication is not that they will not understand but they far more critical problem that others will not understand them, children get extremely self-conscious when trying to speak a foreign language. Add to that the universal French teaching attitude that you correct all errors rather than praise good results and you have a situation where learners are timid and expect themselves to fail. When I tell them that English can be spoken very, very badly and still be understood, most of them don’t believe me at first. And then they hear their fellow students speaking bad English in a dreadful accent and they realize they can understand what the other student is trying to say. And they aren’t even good at English. Question: Why is problem management not a problem solution?
Answer: Problem management is one of the possible effective strategies for dealing with a problem. Some problems cannot be solved. The have to be managed and controlled. The best strategy for any problem is the one that enables you to move on from the problem to other things you want or need to do. In short, problem management and problem solution are different strategies for dealing with problems, and if applied appropriately, equally valid. I have a couple of permanent medical conditions. One, asthma, I have jad since childhood. It is a disability. But because it is well-managed, most of the time I can completely ignore it. I do a gymnastic and a full-body muscle workout every day, I can work for hours with a spade or an axe, and this is because my asthma problem is managed. There is no way to “solve” asthma in the sense of “not having it any more.” In fact, the long term treatment of asthma comes with it's own problems. But as with anything else in real life, there are compromises to make. I accept the side effects. A similar problem exists in risk management. Untrained people assume the goal of risk management is to eliminate all risks Once they learn a little about it, they start to think it's about knowing all risks. But risk management is about strategy and policy. That's what makes it difficult. People in risk management roles accept that they can't eliminate, mitigate, minimise, control or manage every risk. The “Y2K bug” wasn't a problem. It wasn't a problem because it was managed. By this I mean that many of the “solutions” applied were in reality, ugly kludges (one or two were beautiful kludges). I know of at least two which still today require regular intervention by a technician - one to delete log files that a proprietary device operating system can't identify as log files because they use the real date, and the other requires a technician to reset the date in a device to 1974 every January, and correct the date “correction” in a script for the user interface. Question: Hi From the sixteenth century people have published mathematical series that they wrote 'equals pi'. Since they did not know the precise value for pi, on what argument were they able to state that their series = pi?
Answer: No, they do know a precise number. Your problem is in your definition of “precise.” In mathematics, “precise” isn’t an absolute, it’s a number. To put it another way, something is not “either precise or not precise.” In many areas of science and engineering, we routinely tell each other exact numbers that represent “precise.” In one of my areas, cabinetmaking, we talk about “rough” and “precise” measurements, and we all know that “rough” means “about half a finger width” and “precise” means “to the nearest millimetre” and “very precise” means “to the nearest half-millimetre.” In another of my fields, data analysis, often the number put on “precise” is a fraction or a multiple of a standard deviation; sometimes it’s a “normal adjusted sigma” (usually expressed as a number of places of decimals. For PI, many of the practical, real world uses for it can work with the “precise” meaning “expressed as an integer fraction with a denominator under 10. The favourite being 22/7. In many engineering applications, four places of decimals (3.1416) are already more than enough. In short, the basis on which they were able to state that their series = Pi is their strictly proper meaning of the word “precise.”

Answer: I don’t think you understand what “far-fetched” means. Far-fetched means “very distant from any conclusion or opinion that is suggested by the evidence.” It doesn’t mean “involving some really big numbers.” Cosmology necessarily involves very big numbers. But if you gather evidence to gauge the distance between Earth and the furthest visible galaxy from us, you are, necessarily, going to come up with some very big numbers. GN-z11 is 32bn or so light-years from us. It would be far-fetched to suggest it’s anything less than 25bn light-years away, because there would have to be some pretty big errors in the data. Similarly, it would be far-fetched for a journalist to suggest that Mr Trump is innocent on all 34 felony counts, but would not be far-fetched to suggest that he is innocent of felony falsification of business records, and merely guilty of misdemeanor, (name your jurisdiction-appropriate non-felony crimes) on some or all of the 34. The difference between felony and non-felony can come down to perspective… sometimes. Having said that, modern consensus puts the age of the universe at a mere <14bn years, and 27bn is nearly twice that; Rajendra Gupta’s study published a year ago suggests that the bigger number might be correct. It’s important to challenge these things from time to time, but I think it’s worth noting that cosmologists did not think the matter of the age of the Universe was settled. There are still plenty of contradictions in cosmology. So is it far-fetched to suggest the prevailing view may be wrong? No. It’s practically main stream to do so.

Question: Two and two make/makes four. Which one is correct?

It's as if I'm saying, ‘the sum of two and two is four.’ Blindly making the verb plural because the syntax is the same as the Alice and Bob example just isn't how English works. If you use the verb ‘make’ instead, you complicate and confuse (I'm aware some people think the opposite is true, but bear with me.) In ‘two and two make/s four,’ who or what is doing the making? What is this shorthand for? What words are being elided? I can make four from two and two? Four is made from two and two? Two and two, added together, make four? These are (some of) my suggestions, and I like the third one because in this case, the two twos are the subject of the verb and the verb must be plural; ’Egg and bacon, added together, make breakfast.’ However, would I say ‘egg and bacon make breakfast’ or ‘egg and bacon makes breakfast,’ (?) Question: Why do I have such a hard time hearing spoken French? I’ve noticed that this isn’t just French and my ability to hear new languages is not so good. How can I change this?
Answer: This is a very important observation. It all has to do with how language learning actually works. As an infant, you heard all sounds equally loudly. But as you began to learn your native language, the structures in your brain that we call your “auditory system” learned to distinguish between sounds that contain meaning and sounds that do not, based on sounds being made by you and by those around you. Sounds in foreign languages, especially languages that contain many sounds that your native language does not, are actively filtered out by your auditory system. Most linguists go through a phase with every new language they learn, where they can't hear it well if there are a lot of other noises. Although tests say I am bilingual, French is my second language. Although I can read old, middle, early modern and modern French almost as well as I read their English equivalents, I still have trouble following a conversation in French when in the milking shed. Milking machines sound louder when people are speaking French than when they are speaking English. I have noticed the same effect in server-rooms and on factory floors. It's because my auditory system continues to classify machine noise as more meaningful than spoken French. The effect has diminished over time but is still noticeable. What you can do about it is make sure you practice using new languages in noisy places. I find it pretty stressful but it's worthwhile in the long run.

Question: Is a moral, character, values, ethics, respect, and principles development class more important than math, science, and English to teach kids in schools?
Answer: I am hugely in favour of taking an extreme look at ways to reform education. Education in post-industrial, post-nationalist, late-stage capitalist cultures is profoundly broken, even where it is working adequately, and big changes are needed. I don’t pretend to know what those changes might be, so asking yourself and others questions like this one is of profound, public importance. Personally, I think that “practical citizenship” should be a major part of any curriculum, teaching people about their rights, responsibilities, duties, the law, the constitution and political system, economics (both personal, national and international), the truth about societal problems like poverty, violence, oppression of minorities, etc. Many late-stage-capitalist states are fearful of teaching this to their citizens because it will make them too critical of the state’s failures. This is a big issue in both of my countries right now. But I also think that school teaching should focus on preparing people to be better at LEARNING throughout their lives. One of the necessities for this is a strong foundation in communication, math and science. This said, here’s my direct answer to the actual question: Morality is taught to individuals by the society around them. You can’t teach it in the classroom. Character develops over time, in response to the people and events in life. Values are partly acquired from the society and culture around you, partly chosen, in accordance with factors like education, economic advantages and experience. Ethics is a technique. Applying ethics requires the study of ethics. It’s like a special form of logic. However, taking decisions “ethically” in common parlance is a special form of social responsibility, such as a judge who recuses herself because she realizes that there are people involved in a case with whom she has a personal connection. Ethics can theoretically be taught in school, but not at foundational levels. Children should be at least 13/14 before they study ethics. Respect cannot be taught, any more than it can be demanded. It can only be shown. Show respect to people and they will learn to show respect to you and others. The older generation of Americans (those 20+ older than me) seem to have a particular problem with this simple concept, especially where it applies to children (though abusively demanding respect is widespread worldwide). Principles are acquired with experience. They come from having lived long enough to have learned the consequences of certain kinds of action - in particular complex decisions involving uncertain outcomes. Principles cannot be taught. The classroom environment is ideal for learning pure (theoretical) math, and excellent for learning the graphical and practical aspects of math like geometry and engineering. Science REQUIRES A TEACHER. It is a technique for acquiring reliable knowledge that has been developed over multiple generations by many people collaborating for the common good. It’s almost impossible to learn outside of a classroom or in the absence of some sort of educator. English doesn’t really need a teacher. HOWEVER there are enormous advantages to having classes that focus on the understanding, interpretation, use and expression in your native language. This develops fine communication skills, critical and analytical skills, organizational skills. The classroom is an ideal environment for sandboxing these skills which will be of enormous use for the rest of your life.

Question: Does a story still count as fiction if it is a memoir based on something that actually happened?

It presents certain events of his life told as a story through the medium of film. It's mostly not fiction. James Cameron's Titanic is pretty factual when it comes to the ship and what befell it. However, Rose and Jack are completely fictional. This is a mixture of “cinematic fact” and pure fiction. In Moby Dick, the vast majority of the detail of life on a whaling ship is authentic and accurate; Melville had been on the crew of a whaling ship. The rest of the story is made up. In 20 000 Leagues Beneath the Seas, Pierre Arronax is a passenger in a submarine all around the world. Of course, at the time of writing no such vessel existed. However, the geography, oceanography and the (extensive) lists of fish were correct and accurate to the extent of knowledge at the time of writing. The Australian comedian Clive James called his autobiography “Unreliable Memoirs.” The places he described were all real, and many of the people, too. Most of the events probably really happened. But the stories are very funny to read, so it is fair to suppose that James alliwed himself some license; nonetheless, “Unreliable Memoirs” is not usually considered to be fiction. Question: Why do native teachers of European languages like English, French, and Spanish deliberately make their languages look much slower than they actually are, causing everything foreign students have practiced cannot be applied? My Asian friends asked.

In English, however, plenty of teachers do the slowed down version wrongly, instinctively. This is especially true for versions of English which make frequent use of weak vowels, like most UK English variants, and Australian and NZ English (US English varies pretty widely, and many Americans intentionally avoid weak vowels in formal situations so it can seem like they do it a lot less than they do). If when speaking slowly you convert all the weak vowels to strong vowels, which many people seem to do without thinking, you will be pronouncing English differently from how it is normally spoken. This difference between English and French seems to be typical of the difference between stress-timed and syllable timed languages more generally. Syllable-timed languages can be slowed down or sped up (within reason) without changing the relative length of individual syllables.

Question: What is the true nature of consciousness, and how does it emerge from the complex interactions of neurons and synapses in the human brain?
Answer: The advantage conferred by consciousness is missing from Melinda Gwin's answer (which I urge you to read), namely that it enables self-flexibility. Our big brain remains elastic throughout our lives, but because we are conscious of it, we can guide how that elasticity is used, to some extent. This means we are not being passively buffeted by our environment but are actively adapting ourselves to it. This can be a little hit and miss, but across an entire population, statistics suggest it is a huge advantage, unless it gets out of hand. This explains why consciousness happens. But not how it emerges. But it doesn’t emerge from neurons and synapses. That’s not even half the picture. Mammalian brains build structures in response to developmental pressures, some of which come from the inside, and some from the outside. Neurons and synapses have evolved to make those structures. In other words, emergence in biological systems isn’t an “upwards only” process. It acts in all directions at once, with each layer of complexity/abstraction affecting both those above and those below and those adjacent. Consciousness is, in essence, a feedback loop between the structures that enable us to observe ourselves and those that enable us to direct our actions. In short, what we call consciousness is “what it feels like to experience self-awareness.” A point comes in a short explanation like this where many science communicators are tempted to use analogies, but I would rather you ask me pointed questions to show where I have failed to point you in the right direction, because there are no good analogies for mammalian brains other than simpler mammalian brains. And there are no good analogies for consciousness at all.

Question: Is song writing basically like writing free verse poetry and rhyming poetry?
Answer: No. Not even close. I’m sure other people will tell you why free verse poetry can’t possibly work as song lyrics so I’m going to give you a lead vocalist’s reason why the problem goes deeper than the obvious. In pop music, there are several different kinds of lyricists, but as a singer, two types are the best: Those who chose specific words to fit the harmonics or the rhythms of the music they want to write (e.g. Cathy Dennis (who if you don’t know her, has written a lot of the dance/pop that you like of the last 30+ years). Those who construct their lines carefully to ensure that the vocalist has plenty of opportunities to breathe (either in or out) and to build up support (air pressure) for the interpretation intended by the singer (two great examples of this are Paul Simon and George Michael). But other examples can be hugely effective, like the technique of Elton John (take lyrical poetry and construct music for it) or Freddie Mercury (write the melody and lyrics at the same time by singing as you write). At the moment I’m trying for a second time to learn to perform All Star by Smash Mouth. For the musos in the group it’s an annoyingly simple song. But the lyrics are bad. Really bad. They make some sense, but don’t stand up to any deep analysis; the phrasing is unnatural, the syntax is awkward, it’s difficult to remember the lines. I took 25 minutes to learn Kid Charlemagne (Steely Dan) which is a much more difficult song. I’m still learning All Star after three years. That’s a really good example of how a songwriter must have poetical skill. One of the reasons the lyrics of Kid Charlemagne are easy to remember is that they tell a complete story. Where the delivery deviates from the line of the melody during the verses, it’s serving the narrative so you can easily remember exactly what to do and where. But you also have to have a deep understanding of how a lead vocalist interprets lyrics in the music - or, at the very least, be like Bernie Taupin and be really dedicated to lyrical poetry - otherwise you’re going to write nothing but traps for the lead vocalist. Honestly compare All Star to, let’s say “The Kids Aren’t All Right” by the Offspring (stylistically, superficially similar, and from adjacent years I think, that’s why I’m choosing them) and you’ll see exactly how to do lyrics for this kind of music. Question: Why is graffiti totally legal if your name is "Banksy", but totally illegal for everyone else?
Answer: Graffiti is special. When I was a child, in London, some of the graffiti was really special. Random artists doing amazing stuff; figurative, evocative, cheerful colours, amazing shading. I loved it back then. The fact it was illegal and “vandalism” was relevant, of course. If you were poor or non-white, London could be a really awful place in those days. The graffiti had (and still has) the same cultural value and cultural importance of cave and rock art that’s centuries old. It’s about a human desire to express the inexpressible, to communicate to anyone who will hear it, the cri de coeur that “I too, am a person.” When I moved to France, I was faintly horrified. The goal of most graffiti here isn’t street art. It’s provocative defacement whose primary challenge is to place your “tag” or the tag of your gang, in a highly visible, but also dangerously inaccessible place. This isn’t to say it isn’t sometimes motivated by the desire of disadvantaged people to be noticed, to be heard, and in some way have some effect on the smug elites who keep them down. It also isn’t to say that sometimes the locations where they manage to get their tags to are genuinely awe-inspiring. But the art itself is homemade tattoo levels of bad. I find that troubling. So why is graffiti illegal? Because that’s the point. Historically, graffiti is done by people who are neglected or oppressed by the system. It’s a protest, no matter how inarticulate it may sometimes be. Illegality is the whole point. Banksy is not a graffiti artist. His work is “guerrilla art” akin to yarn-bombing. And hey, he’s managed to make a reputation and a career from it and that, frankly is a good thing for the world. But that’s also the reason it isn’t illegal: the rich can profit from Banksy’s art (regardless of how much he might try to satirize that), so they accept it. If the rich start one day profiting from graffiti, people will stop doing it, I hope.

Question: How is AI killing software engineers? What can we do to stop it?
Answer: For LLM based AI (the type of AI that most people are familiar with) to write software, it needs to be able to draw on large, parallel code bases written in languages that haven't changed much in the last 30 years or so. Now… I happen to have been using VBA (visual basic for applications) since I was 17, that’s 33 years, and in that time it's undergone a few changes and a couple of actual improvements (precise variable scope, for instance). Also, because VBA is used in a very narrow but extremely common niche, the same problems have been solved countless times. So if LLM can code, it must, surely, be able to write a VBA function that matches columns in an Excel spreadsheet with corresponding columns in an Access database and find gaps in the data. Yeah no. Not even close. Not even if I supply it with the object I want used in the output, and the full specifications of the WorkSheet and the Table. In fact it makes both trivial errors that even a VBA programmer wouldn't make, like scoping errors and mismatched types (which will just make VBA refuse to run), and it gives properties and methods to objects that don't have them. What makes the best programmers so good is all the obscure details they have learned over the years, often this is what to avoid (for a table that gets it's data from a linked spreadsheet, should I use an ADODB or a DAO object? Should I use Recordset or Recordset2?). Because of the way that AI is taught, it's impossible for it to know what it shouldn't do. Also, of course, VBA has long been the language of dabblers. So a significant proportion of the VBA in the wild is very, very bad. AI has no way to know this. If the same error has been committed multiple times by humans, AI will also commit the error. So here's a prediction: When an AI writes a programming language, its compiler, its decompiler, its debugger and all its interfaces/interoperability, AI will subsequent to that be able to replace software engineers. Until then, I reckon it may eventually be quite a useful tool for brainstorming approaches to common programming requirements. As of right now tho, competent programmers work faster without it, and for that to change, AI has to acquire a type of intelligence it does not yet have.

Question: How do you write the humming sound for "yes" in English: "Mmhum," "Uhmhum," "mmhumm," or "Uh huh"? Are these official words in English? What part of speech are they?

Question: Why do some programmers like to use technobabble to sound smart?

Question: Would you rather use a metronome with pure clicks or metronomes with drum patterns?
Answer: I've had multiple music teachers tell me to use a metronome. And then watched me play along with and without a metronome. And then tell me not to bother with a metronome. However, for woodwind, I do use a tuning app for some pf my exercises as although my ear is good, it's not precise enough for, for example, jumping more than an octave on the clarinet with a Jazz mouthpiece. One thing all my teachers have agreed on: clicks are best. Why? Because a metronome is supposed to teach you timing, that you can then use while performing without a metronome. If you use drum patterns, you will end up doing what many musicians do naturally, which is adapt your timing to specific cues in the drumming pattern. As a result you will need the drums to be able to keep time. This means the moment you have a solo, or there's a caesura to play through, you will not be able to keep time. Play something wildly simple (like Au Claire de la Lune or Sing a Song of Sixpence) with a metronome, and time it precisely. Play it again without the metronome, also with a timer. Practice alternating between with and without until it takes exactly the same amount of time. (I've used this technique to test my rhythm, too)

Question: Why is it that even after 25 years, the progress bars and 'remaining time' estimates of software installations of Microsoft and others so hilariously wrong? Installed iOS 17.3 today and the '0 seconds remaining' stayed on for 2 minutes!

Our progress bar was very simple; every something seconds (the period was based on how long it took for users to get antsy and divide by two) it would check the time passed since data was last received. If the delay was acceptable, it would increase the progress counter by a random amount. Once the counter got past 75%, from time to time there was either a message “new data, updating…” or “additional data required.” And the counter would drop by between 15% and 25%. Sometimes we'd ask users how the dowloads were going “on your system” and they'd tell us “oh, there was a big update today” or “not too much additional data today.” The goal of this was as stated. We (by which I mean some of my very smart colleagues, not me) concluded that since most of our users had no idea at all of what was going on, they needed something reassuring, but also vaguely analogous to reality. I think our solution was superior to ones that actually counted real kilobits per second.

Question: Any ideas for a novel that actually has enough content so I don't accidentally turn it into a short story?

From time to time I get an author to write a sentence about their book starting with the words: “What does it feel like when… “ and ending with a questionmark, e.g. What does it feel like when you think you have everything you need to make your life complete, then, through no fault of your own, you lose it all, but through grit and determination, you get it all back, only to lose it all again, this time through your own foolishness, but through the events and people you meet during all of this, you realize that you never really needed all that, and that what you really need is something else, and now all you have left to do is explore that new horizon? Suppose that (or something like it) us what you want to SAY with your story. Can’t do it with a short story. You have to construct the story that will convey that message, that question, that emotional experience. That’s what it’s about. As for ideas, I have more of those than you could possibly use, but that’s because it’s been my job for the best part of two decades to teach people how to construct a novel, starting with what you want (or need) your work to say, creating an emotional experience from that, and choosing the ideas, the setting, the characters, the events, and building the story that will deliver that experience to the reader. The ideas are just part of the process, and not the hardest part. For many writers, the hardest part is finding out what they are trying to say. It’s not at all unusual to discover this by writing a lot of short stories and never being completely satisfied with them.

Question: Are there cases where repairing a corrupted MS Word file exacerbates the problem rather than resolving it?

Question: I usually write every letter in a word separately and find this way too slow. Is there a faster way to write like the letters are linked?
Answer: SMW. There is a widespread belief that cursive script makes handwriting faster. So prevalent is this belief that the Wikipedia article you are currently running to in order to “prove me wrong” contradicts itself repeatedly on this point. Testing has repeatedly shown that with modern writing implements, cursive is no faster. But with quills, inkpens and early fountain-pens, cursive was faster. Not because you can form the letters any faster, but because ink-use is more efficient, ink flow is more regular, blotting and/or sanding are done less often, and spills, soaks and runs occur less. All this is because the goal of cursive is to avoid lifting the nib from the paper. WYLTKM? (If not, skip to the paragraph that's starts with ‘Modern ink pens…’) It's all about capillary action. The ink fills the nib of an inkpen through one or (sometimes) two very narrow channels, through capillary action. Contact of the nib with the paper continues capillary flow. If you lift the nib, the flow stops. In a quill, this is a very big problem because the pithy interior of the quill acts like a sponge, and if the ink is no longer flowing onto the page, it soaks back up into the depleted reservoir, because just like a sponge, the distribution of ink in the reservoir tends to equalize across its entire volume, through, YGI, capillary action. Most modern ink pens exploit the properties of different arrangements of fibres and/or very small tubes to ensure that capillary flow is always (or mostly always) towards the nib. Others (like ballpoints) use direct transfer. Blotting and sanding isn't necessary. Spills and runs and wads and other defects that could mean having to start over, don't happen at all. Now… a lot of people really love cursive, and I don't begrudge them it. But this does cause them to make claims about its worth that are demonstrably untrue. When done with skill, it can produce elegant text that is agreeable to read. However many forms of cursive (including the one still taught in French schools which may explain why I have a bee in my bonnet) have been shown in testing to be more difficult to read than others, and all forms of non cursive are more likely to be legible. TL;DR, such as it is, is this: whatever script you use, the only reliable ways to hand write faster are to use good quality writing implements and put in more time practicing your writing. Personal footnote: Just as some people really love cursive and are very skilled at it, and this skews their opinion of it's virtues, you should know that was functionally illiterate until age 8 (in education, we don't use the term “illiterate” for children, but the strictly correct terminology gives a very wrong impression), and only caught up with (and subsequently overtook) my reading and writing age when I was around 10/11 years old. As a result, throughout my education my handwriting was poor, and at University I typed all my assignments. I'm adding this because it may seem as if I have a bias against handwriting, and perhaps I do. However I later studied calligraphy. I handwrite all my notes for my day-job, so I hand write quite a lot more than most people of working age, although most of what I write is only for me to read. My bias against it centres on how the education system prioritizes it over typing (and communication skills in general), forcing children to waste time that could be better spent learning skills they will actually use. To this day, there are teachers in Lycées who refuse to accept typewritten assignments. I have talked to them about it. They come across childishly obtuse.

Question: How do harmonica players remember different keys and positions? They just do or they don't and just remember the hole tabs?
Answer: Speaking for myself, I know what I want to play, and I choose the harmonica that will enable me to play it Mostly I play in 2nd position (“cross harp”) but there are a few songs where 1st, 3rd or 4th is needed. Jazz manouche sometimes requires more than one harp and Breton folk and sea shanties often need natural minors (I don't use bends for those notes in folk as it spoils the timbre). So how do I remember which harp goes with which song? I don't. I work it out while rehearsing, sometimes while preparing on my own, and then I write it down. How do I remember which notes are where and when? I don't do that consciously at all. Once you are in the song, you pick up the tonic and the scale (and sometimes the mode) from the musicians around you. From there I just know what to play, and if I have the right harmonica in my mouth, I will play whatever note I have in mind. For most songs, I prepare a few stings, riffs, melodic sections and harmonic phrases, but improvise my solos around set phrases that I think sit well with the song. I don't know what a hole tab is, but I can guess. I think if you're using any sort of tab, you need to practice more, either until you can sight-read sheet music, or until you can memorise a song and play the notes you have in mind. Memorizing which holes to blow or draw seems like an extra layer of complication making the whole process more difficult.

Question: Why was I brought up with the rules for writing saying that you should never start a sentence with and, but, or because? Yet it really complicates the way you write sometimes, and I noticed in novels they ignore these supposed rules?
Answer: Why were you taught these rules seems to be your question, and the answer goes back to when mass public education was being conceived, depending on where you live, generally before 1950, but in most places sometime between 1880 and 1930. Teaching these rules was a conscious choice, based not upon what people thought was “correct” — the highly educated minority at that time never even wondered if their grammar was “correct” — but based on the minimum standard of written communication they expected the majority of people to need. Rules relating to not starting sentences with conjunctions are specifically because the expectation was that people with that level of education would rarely if ever write more than one sentence at a time, so to be sure of avoiding error, they should learn only one way to construct complex sentences. Since conjunctions exist to join the clauses of complex sentences, the easiest structure to remember is one where the conjunction is placed literally between the clauses. This is based on a theory of education that persists to this day but is not often enough revealed to pupils and students: that as you progress, rules you learned when you were younger get replaced by guidelines, methods, and a deeper understanding. In both my countries, there have been periods of time where, especially in teaching grammar, teachers themselves lost sight of the purpose of the rules taught to children, and there are entire generations convinced they know the only right way to use their language. You still see a lot of those people on Quora, and many of them make valuable contributions. So sticking to these rules is demonstrably a good thing. It just isn't necessary if you are the master of your own syntax.

Question: What should I, a person who has no idea about coding, say to a coder to make them happy?
Answer: Some people are comfortable with being identified by the thing that they do. Many (including me) are not. For instance, I don’t mind if someone calls me an engineer, although I consider that inaccurate. In two very specific, narrow ways, I often have to apply engineering principles to my day job. I would not like to be called “a coder.” It would be like calling an artist who makes sculptures from wood “a chiseler.” But I suspect your question comes from a place of sensitivity, and my mood can be bound up in my current project, whatever that might be. If you’re sensitive to that, then the best thing you can do is some version of each of the following: #1 you: “how’s it going?” them : “I’m concentrating…” you: “sorry to disturb you…” #2 you: “how’s it going?” them: “I’m doing this [enthusiastic but only mildly comprehensible explanation] thing!” you: “sounds like satisfying work. Can I get you anything?” #3 you: “how’s it going?” them: “it’s okay. A bit of a chore.” you: “I’m available if you want to do something else to get your mind off it for a while…” #4 you: “how’s it going?” them: “ugh. I’m getting nowhere, but I have to get this finished.” you: “Can I get you anything?” #5 you: “how’s it going?” them: “ugh, I’m getting nowhere… “ pause you: “maybe take a break? I’m available…” Each one of these is an example of being sensitive to their relationship with their work, being supportive, considerate and available, while allowing them to decide how to deal with the situation. That is a great way to make someone happy, but really applies to any occupation that requires bursts of intense concentration, and also often involves frustration and a degree of drudgery. That kind of activity does attract certain types of personality, and often they’re people who while their mind is on one thing, don’t give much attention to articulating their feelings, but also don’t filter them, so if you’re sensitive, you’ll know how they feel. It’s also a good playbook to avoid making them unhappy, by giving them space when they need it, providing hydration, and being available for them when they are available. Couples where both people code often end up synchronizing their downtime. If one has this sort of job and the other does not, it’s important for both to be aware of and talk about this dynamic.

Question: Will speaking English help make the German language easy to learn?
Answer: This question, and variations of it, seems to attract answers based on supposed arguments for why it should be, based in a common descent, and on lexical (and other) linguistic similarities. But these answers ignore three key details: #1. All modern European languages have a long history of being taught to foreigners, through very similar education traditions and very similar classroom techniques. This means if you are truly monolingual you will likely find all the major European equally easy/difficult. It's when you come to learn a third language that features of the language start to make a difference, and for anglophones that often depends on the grammar of your second language eing similar to the third. 2# A huge proportion of Germans speak English at CERCL level B1 or better. This is a huge advantage to anglophones trying to learn German in Germany, but it also means that online resources to help English speakers to learn German are numerous, rich, detailed, effective and highly accessible. 3# Actual statistical evidence (from Germany) shows that English speakers who move to Germany are among the fastest foreigners at learning to speak German. TBH, as a language educator, only point #3 is relevant in answering this question. A conclusive reason for why it might be so would require exhaustive large scale research to get an answer we don't really need. Question: Is the following sentence grammatically correct…"If you're going to level cheap shots at strangers, at least spell them correctly." I think "them" is used incorrectly here…doesn't "them" refer to "strangers" and not "cheap shots"?
Answer: No, it refers to the cheap shots. This is fundamental to how English works: all nouns are not created equal. When a noun is introduced to a sentence, there is a hierarchy that is established which is based partly on the order of the nouns, and partly on their relationship with the verb. Did you know for example that this is the MAIN REASON for the use of the passive voice in English? It ensures the most important noun has the most important relationship with the verb. Usually, a pronouns is lower in the hierarchy than a named noun. The exception is when the pronoun is standing in for the main subject of a paragraph. We don’t know if that’s the case here, but it doesn’t look like it. So the nouns are “cheap shots” and “strangers.” “Cheap shots” is the direct object of the verb. This places it much higher in the ranking than “strangers” whose relationship to the verb is mediated by a preposition via the direct object (you can think of this as making it “further away” from the verb). So the first assumption of an English speaker is that the pronoun “them” refers to the “cheap shots.” If that is not the intent, then the sentence needs to be rewritten.

Where do people frequently go wrong in pancake batter: Get in the habit of tasting your batter. Some people insist you have to leave the batter to stand before cooking but you don't; you can use it immediately; you just get slightly different (but equally good) pancakes. The main error when cooking is failing to match pan temperature to pancake thickness; a very thin pancake needs a hotter pan. Thin is not inherently better. The sweeter the batter, the thinner the pancake should be. Your pan does not need to be swimming with oil. But it does need to be CLEAN, smooth and hot, and the handle must not be loose. Question: Should schools place a heavy emphasis on grammar when teaching English as a second language? Or should more emphasis be put on real-life application for communicative purposes?
Answer: tl;dr: emphatically NO grammar. In countries which use the same (or very similar) alphabet, English should be taught in schools (assuming they start learning aged between 7 and 10) as follows: The purpose of this approach is to minimize resistance to English which is almost always caused by discussion of grammar, syntax and (especially) tenses if such discussions occur before the student is orally functional. Adult learners can easily compress this into 2 to 3 years part-time. Orally, English is very easy to learn because it is so prevalent and available worldwide. However, English spelling is idiotic, and we could actually do something about that, but we don’t because the same spellings are pronounced differently worldwide (and even within some quite small countries). English grammar is a topic of permanent debate. Tenses are nightmarishly difficult to analyse without first knowing how to use them. This is the worst error of English teaching historically: the idea that students can learn to use the tenses correctly if they are explained first. Doing this actively creates resistance because it makes many students think they will never be able to master it, because the explanation seems so counter-intuitive or confusing. What they don’t realize is that much of English grammar can only be explained badly. It’s neither the student nor the explanation that is at fault. The best way to avoid this resistance is to teach tense orally with NO EXPLANATION first. Once your students can manage both aspects in past, present and future, those who don’t get the grammatical analysis can safely ignore it. Which is what most native English speakers do. Seems to work okay for them.

Answer: This triggers my software PM instincts to reply: “question for the questioner: do you want to build an LMS to use it, or do you want to create an LMS product you want to sell?” If the former, just don't. The LMS marketplace is by no means saturated but if you need one, there will be one that meets your needs or can be readily customised to do so. If the latter… well, the market isn't saturated so it isn't the worst idea, but if you're hoping to develop a product you already know which ones you want to compete with; in fact, as critical path research you have already bought licences and set up servers running each of your future competitors, and will have already started to RE and cross specify them to derive your core requirements. You probably already have a general design. And you've probably hired a consultant software architect to help you estimate at the very least, the project scale and scope, which might result in a man-hours ballpark to reach a POC, and thence a demo to put in front of potential investors. For info, I'm not a software PM any more but expert LMS knowledge for both possibilities and choice when designing training programmes is in my job description so I'm up to date on this stuff.

Question: Many singers don’t even understand music theory. How could they write so many good songs?
Answer: I read music very slowly; if I already know the song, I can use sheet music to follow along, which is very useful in longer pieces, but I can't sight-read like the classically trained musicians most of my teachers have been. My clarinet teacher can work out the key to a song, slowly, and then improvise an accompaniment to it on the piano using techniques she learned during her formal musical education. I can play along with a song instantly on the clarinet, finding root notes by ear. She can't. I can choose which diatonic harmonica to use to play along with a song (I can usually narrow it down to one of three likely keys then test them.) More complex and interesting music can require more than one harmonica - a lot of Magyar gypsy music requires three harmonicas in the same key, but one major, one h minor and one n minor. I can improvise a solo on several instruments. One of the biggest differences between me and my clarinet teacher, where she had as much trouble understanding what I was doing as I did what she was doing is the relationship between tones (notes) and fingerings. There are several sizes of clarinet, snd each is “in a different key.” This is in scare quotes because it's not a different key the way a diatonic harmonica is. A diatonic harmojica has all the notes of only one scale. Try to play a different scale and some notes will be missing. You can play any scale on any clarinet. But different clarinets play a different scale with the same fingerings. Here's where my teacher (and most classically trained clarinetists) differs from me: when she reads music, the notes on rhe page tell her hands which fingering to play. When I read music, the notes tell me which sounds to make, and my hands find the fingering on their own. All I need is an arpeggio. (Or a pentatonic). This gives her a huge advantage playing classical music, where a stronger reed is used, and a more constant air pressure and an inflexible embouchure is what propagates the very distinctive (and pure) sound of the classical clarinet. It gives me a huge advantage playing jazz because I can go instantly from sounds in my head to sounds on the instrument. If she wants to switch to a different size of clarinet, she has to use sheet music transposed into a different key, so that the fingerings correspond to the correct notes. I do not need different sheet music. I can switch between any of the wind instruments I can play, and all I need are the root notes. Fingering takes care of itself. What I'm saying is that these two very different ways to approach music have major consequences for the type of music you can learn to play well. It is highly unlikely I will ever come close to the quality of tone that my teacher has in classical pieces. She will likely never be able to improvise a solo to a song she is hearing for the first time. To classically trained musicians, jazz seems extremely complex because they think about music analytically. To jazz musicians, it's right when it feels right. Good jazz is the stuff where classically trained musicians can analyse it and tell you a lot of technical terms for all the clever, subtle stuff the musicians are doing. Without knowing they are doing it. For most jazz musicians, classical music theory creates needless layers of complexity and distance between the player and the music. But the reality is that different approaches to music suit different people. That's the answer to your question. Sorry for the long walk.

Question: How do they call Santa Claus in the United Kingdom?
Answer: When I was very small we were expressly forbidden from using the name “Santa Claus,” especially if pronounced the American way. We were told that: A) they aren't the same person, and B) in Emglish he is called Saint Nicholas In a few places in the UK over the last couple of hundred years, a religious divide (between AC and CofE) determined whether you said Saint Nicholas or Father Christmas, though iin my family no one was particularly religious other than my paternal grandmother who would have been pretty shocked had I or my sisters referred to “Santa Claws.”

Question: Why didn’t Doctor Who appear in the 2012 Olympics ceremony? Is Doctor Who culturally less significant than Rowan Atkinson?
Answer: In one of Michael Moorcock's “Jerry Cornelius” books, written in the 1970s, Jerry attends a fancy-dress party where the theme is “folk heroes.” Obviously there's at least one Robin Hood. But there's also a Dr Who.* Because even in the 1970s, the Doctor was arguably a folk hero, and very much part of national culture and the experience of growing up in the UK. Mr Bean is much less of a cultural icon in the UK than Edmund Blackadder (another of Atkinson’s characters). Blackadder is cultually and historically important in a way that Mr Bean just isn't. Mr Bean is a well-known brand worldwide. But would you put him on the cover of Sargent Pepper? I don't think so. * The modern fandom is very picky about the idea that Dr Who is the name of the show, not the character. Back in the 1970s, we were not so fussy, and certainly never got butthurt over it.

Question: Why do people have such high prices for Starbucks coffee when McDonald's coffee is good and a lot cheaper?
Answer: McDonald's coffee is terrible. It's not the absolute worst of fast food coffees but it is very bad. Starbucks coffee is merely burnt. Historically, coffee merchants would burn the beans during torrefaction on purpose and call it dark roast, to disguise the fact they were buying the cheapest beans currently available; burning the coffee hides the flavour, so when they switch suppliers you don't notice a change of flavour. I have very little doubt that Starbucks is doing the same, but it doesn't matter since they sell very little actual coffee. Their customers pay the high prices for the fancy ingredients that the coffee is flavoured with, and for the even fancier beverage names. I'm not a coffee snob. I drink coffee with my breakfast once a week from La Brioche Dorée which is a chain of patisseries in France (and a few EU cities) and their coffee is much better than Starbucks. Not because it's especially good. It just isn't burnt. Coffee in most French cafés is made in a traditional Italian café espresso machine by Lavazza or Segafredo or others, and is almost always better and cheaper than Starbucks.

Question: How can I learn JavaScript in one day?
Answer: If you are already comfortable with another language that has C - like syntax… If you are already proficient in another sparse scripting or scriptlike language like LUA, perl or Python… If you have already used some other technology to manipulate web content (i.e. a webserver running php or asp.net)… If you are comfortable with weak typing… If you are comfortable with runtime compiling… If your math skills are well above average… If you have a really great grasp of what actually happens within the built-in functions and libraries of other languages… If you are really, really disciplined when it comes to writing conforming, readable code but are comfortable wading through the opposite… If you can look up a problem on stack exchange, and understand answers written in a language you don't know or don't know well, and then apply them in a language you do know well… If you know the basics of markup languages and the main principles of the DOM… … if ALL OF THIS is you, JavaScript in a day is trivial. You will barely notice it. You'll probably still fall into one or two basic pitfalls (e.g. side effects, weak types that are “guessed” even in function calls, scope, games with the defer keyword…), but this is normal. An experienced programmer should have no serious difficulties with JS. If all those ifs don't describe you, you can still learn JS in a matter of weeks if you apply yourself. No other language has such a wide variety and quantity of accessible real world examples. Runtime compiling and jit debugging is really simple for those folks who learn by debugging. JS can even borrow DOM functionality to behave like a hierarchical OO language if that's what you prefer. I really, really like JS. But I've been working with it since 1998.

Question: Which computer language is easy to learn for non-professionals?
Answer: JavaScript. JavaScript has some oddities but there are a number of reasons it's easy to learn: It's been fashionable, pretty much since the first version of JS was released, to criticise JS. Mostly this is the result of selective demagogy, and should be ignored. But you do have to read the specification, and NEVER use any built in function or operator without reading the official documentation. JS is surprisingly rich in pitfalls-for-the-unwary for such a small language.

Name: Harry Dewulf
Question: Is learning JavaScript good?
Answer: Yes. It is very good. If you read the specifications and the full documentation of all the built-in keywords and symbols, you will have learned a valuable programmer’s skill and you will write JS well and read it better. If you rely only on reading existing code, examples on stack exchange and occasionally glance at a reference site, you will write bad JS. Somewhere on DailyWTF there is an article that references my wrapper for parseInt that adds the optional argument if it isn't supplied, which I created because most of my colleagues had never read the specifications and made a dangerous assumption that occasionally yielded unexpected values. Learning JavaScript teaches you via a relatively terse, poor language, the value of reading both the specifications and the documentation - and the power that comes from knowing it.

Question: Do you think that people who want to live in England, should have to learn to speak English?
Answer: Not being proficient in the local language is amything from a disadvantage to a risk. In France, in order to obtain citizenship you have to pass an exam in French. This is for your own legal protection; it ensures that you have the minimum proficiency to be able to comprehend the citizenship documentation, and ensure you can, for example, understand an employment contract and not be exploited or scammed. So to benefit from opportunities and to avoid all sorts of risks, learning the local language conveys a range pf practical, legal and social advantages all of which will improve your economic prospects. But the wording of your question suggests that this practical approach doesn't feed the controversy you're angling for.
